children: The fourth quarter has historically been the S&P 500’s (
) strongest stretch of the year, and that record is back in focus as October opens with stocks still near record territory and Treasury yields at multi-decade highs.

Carson Investment Research spotlighted data from 1950 through 2025 showing the index rising an average of 4.2% in the fourth quarter, more than double the average gain in either of the first two quarters and well ahead of the third quarter’s 0.8%. The index finished the quarter higher 80.3% of the time, compared with roughly 62% to 63% in the other three. The median fourth-quarter gain over that span was 5.2%.

The more recent record is stronger still. Over the past 13 years, the S&P 500 rose in 12 fourth quarters, a 92.3% hit rate, with an average gain of 5.4% and a median of 6.5%. The sole decline was in 2018, when the index fell 14%. Gains elsewhere in that window ran as high as 11.7% in 2020 and 11.2% in 2023, though the last two fourth quarters were more modest, at 2.1% in 2024 and 2.3% in 2025.
That history arrives against a less comfortable backdrop. On Thursday the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield

pushed above 5.3%, its highest level since 2002, as a bond selloff weighed on equities even with the S&P 500 still within a few percent of its record. A government bond yield north of 5% raises the hurdle for richly valued shares, leaving investors to weigh a favorable seasonal pattern against higher discount rates and still-elevated index levels.

Seasonality is a tendency, not a timetable. The fourth quarter has been the market’s best quarter on average, and it has finished higher far more often than not. It has also produced the worst drawdown of the past 13 years. How 2026 finishes will depend less on the calendar than on whether earnings can keep pace with yields that have not been this high in more than two decades.

title: The S&P’s strongest historical quarter starts with yields at multi decade highs
